analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: Introduced the day after the 2003 Medicare drug law was signed, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug law created the new Part D benefit but barred the government from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill, introduced by Senator Daschle the day after that law was signed, would have deleted that ban and directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate drug prices on behalf of tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries, the way the VA and other federal agencies already do when buying in bulk. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who pay out-of-pocket costs tied to the prices of their prescriptions, and taxpayers, who help fund the Part D benefit. If the Secretary could negotiate lower prices the way other federal bulk buyers do, both would pay less for the same drugs. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the 'noninterference' provision of the new Medicare Part D law, which had expressly forbidden the government from interfering with negotiations between drug plans and manufacturers.
Gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to negotiate contracts with manufacturers of covered Part D drugs, so beneficiaries 'pay the lowest possible price'.

Bases the Secretary's authority on that of other federal entities that buy prescription drugs in bulk, such as the Department of Veterans Affairs, which has long negotiated much lower prices for the same medicines.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare revenues would be reduced if the government used its bargaining power to push prices down. Supporters of the industry also argued that lower returns could reduce investment in new drug development over time. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes negotiation but does not spell out hard price targets or enforcement mechanisms, so the savings would have depended entirely on how aggressively the Secretary of the moment used the new authority.

Drug manufacturers and their allies argued that government negotiation amounts to price-setting that would reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines, an objection any honest supporter of the bill would have to weigh.

The bill amended a drug benefit that had just been enacted weeks earlier, so the full design and costs of Part D had not yet been tested before Congress would have been asked to rework its central cost-control provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the core question, the bill sided with the 40-plus million Americans on Medicare over the most profitable industry in the country: it would have ended the legal guarantee that the government pays whatever drugmakers charge. The honest costs are the industry's argument about research investment and the bill's thin design — it authorizes bargaining without specifying hard price benchmarks, so its real-world savings would have hinged on enforcement. It is a straightforward cost-containment bill whose main defect is brevity, not design.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced the day after the 2003 Medicare drug law was signed, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there — no markup, no vote, no floor action — until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the bill on December 9, 2003, one day after the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act was enacted with its ban on government price negotiation.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.
Nineteen Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no committee markup, no vote, no floor consideration — before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
The ban on Medicare price negotiation that this bill targeted remained in law for nearly two more decades, until Congress authorized Medicare negotiation in 2022.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which kept the statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation in place and continued charging the government's largest health program market prices for another two decades. Medicare beneficiaries paid Part D prices based on those un-negotiated rates.

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 9, 2003, the day after the Medicare drug law was signed, to strike its ban on government price negotiation.

for.name: 19 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Stabenow, Graham of Florida, Kennedy, Pryor, Dorgan, Boxer, Lautenberg, Bingaman, Mikulski, Johnson, Schumer, Kohl, Cantwell, and Rockefeller.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a markup or vote on it, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price negotiation and supported the noninterference ban in the newly enacted Medicare drug law that this bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, in line with the party split that had just produced the 2003 Medicare law, which passed with the ban on negotiation intact.

industries.note: The bill would have given Medicare the power to negotiate prices for the drugs it buys for tens of millions of beneficiaries, directly threatening the industry's revenue in its largest government program. The industry's interest lay in keeping the just-enacted ban on negotiation, which the bill would have repealed.

Plans administering the Part D benefit would pay manufacturers less under negotiated prices, though the bill leaves the private-plan structure of Part D — and the plans' role as intermediaries — untouched. Their interest in lower drug costs runs alongside beneficiaries'.
